10	False Start Penalties of
11	Offensive Linemen in the
12	National Football League
13	(NFL)
14	
15	
16	James K. Bowman1 , Daniel Krywaruczenko2,
17	Brandon G. De Flon3, and R. Thomas Boone4
18	
19	
20	
21	Abstract
22	Each year in the United States, many factors are considered in the National Football
23	League’s draft process, including scouting reports, interviews, medical tests, and
24	measures of players’ strength, speed, anthropometry, and personality. Recently, an
25	increased emphasis has been placed on players’ psychometrically measured cognitive
26	abilities. Historically, offensive linemen have been excluded from NFL research, since
27	they do not have individual performance statistics. In this study, we attempted to ﬁll
28	that research gap by investigating correlates of offensive linemen’s measured vigilance/
29	impulsivity. We obtained archival player data from 85 offensive linemen in the years
30	from 2014–2021 prior to each of these players’ NFL draft. We then used false start
31	penalties per game (FSPG) as an index of their vigilance/impulsivity (and general
32	success) on the ﬁeld, and we related those values to Reaction Time tests through
33	hierarchical multiple regression analyses. After controlling for draft placement, these
34	players’ higher accuracy on a Choice Reaction Time task accounted for a statistically
35	
36	1
37	  Ofﬁce of Pupil Personnel Services, Great Neck Public Schools, Great Neck, NY, USA
38	2
39	  Department of Sports Management, Centenary College of Louisiana, Shreveport, LA, USA
40	3
41	  Independent Researcher, Albuquerque, NM, USA
42	4
43	  Department of Provost Ofﬁce, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, North Dartmouth, MA, USA
44	
45	Corresponding Author:
46	James K. Bowman, Ofﬁce of Pupil Personnel Services, Great Neck Public Schools, 140 Clover Drive, Great
47	Neck, NY 11020-1606, NY, USA.
48	Email: jbowman@greatneck.k12.ny.us
49	 2                                                        Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
50	
51	signiﬁcant percentage of the variance associated with their FSPG statistics. We discuss
52	the practical utility for player development of these and other cognitive assessments
53	now used in the NFL.
54	
55	
56	Keywords
57	cognition in sport, american football, nﬂ draft, reaction time
58	
59	
60	
61	Introduction
62	At the start of the 2023 American football season, the aggregate value of the National
63	Football League (NFL) was estimated at $163 billion, with the value of the average
64	team placed at $5.1 billion (Ozanian & Teitelbaum, 2023). In the context of these major
65	economic pressures, all 32 NFL teams go to great lengths each year to compete for a
66	championship, including each team’s heavy investment in predicting and improving
67	individual player’s athletic performance.
68	   The annual talent identiﬁcation process for players entering the NFL draft includes a
69	review of the players’ anthropometric measurements and physical attributes (e.g.,
70	statistics related to their size, strength, and speed) and measures of their psychological
71	functioning, including both their cognitive abilities and personality functioning. The
72	development, measurement quality, and practical utility of both these physical and
73	psychological measures have important limitations. For instance, research to date has
74	shown inconsistent relationships between player performance on isolated physical tests
75	and their subsequent NFL game performance (Lyons et al., 2011). Similarly, per-
76	sonality assessments have limitations, including a self-report bias that can contribute to
77	inaccurate personality assessment (Roth et al., 1986). Additionally, since longitudinal
78	research has shown that changes in personality tend to correlate with changes in life
79	satisfaction, work environment, and socioeconomic status over time (Boyce et al.,
80	2012; Le et al., 2014), an athlete whose personal wealth is changed dramatically by a
81	multi-million-dollar NFL contract can experience major changes from initial per-
82	sonality ﬁndings.
83	   Perhaps the domain with the greatest research advancements in recent years is
84	cognitive functioning. Considerable research over 40+ years has shown relationships
85	between cognitive functioning and athletic performance (Farrow et al., 1998; Faubert,
86	2013; Vaeyens et al., 2008). For instance, Jacobson and Matthaeus (2014) found that
87	athletes scored signiﬁcantly higher on measures of inhibition and problem-solving than
88	non-athletes, and, in a meta-analysis conducted by Voss et al. (2010), athletes scored
89	higher than non-athletes on measures of processing speed and varied cognitive at-
90	tention tasks. Some researchers and theorists have argued that the cognitive domain
91	may be the most important distinguishing factor between elite and non-elite athletes
92	(Zaichkowsky & Peterson, 2018). Yet, for decades, the Wonderlic Personnel Test was
93	the sole NFL measure of intellectual ability (Wonderlic, 2013), even while its scores
94	 Bowman et al.                                                                           3
95	
96	have not shown predictive validity with respect to NFL player performance (Kuzmits &
97	Adams, 2008; Lyons et al., 2009). This seemingly led to the NFL’s 2022 announcement
98	that the Wonderlic Personnel Test would no longer be administered to all prospective
99	players at the NFL Scouting Combine (O’Connell, 2022).
100	   Among new cognitive tests developed for use with prospective NFL players, the
101	Player Assessment Test (PAT; Siena Consulting, 2013) was designed to measure
102	learning styles, decision-making skills, core intellect, and the ability to respond to
103	unexpected stimuli (Breer, 2013; Howard, 2013). Unfortunately, despite the 10-year
104	history of the PAT, there are no peer-reviewed research studies that have identiﬁed
105	signiﬁcant relationships between scores on factors of the PAT and aspects of NFL game
106	performance. Other, newer cognitive measures (e.g., APTUS, S2) also lack published
107	empirical support for NFL applications.
108	   The one cognitive assessment tool with demonstrated signiﬁcant relationships
109	between test scores and NFL performance is the Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ;
110	Bowman et al., 2020; Boone, 2024). The AIQ, based on the most empirically supported
111	theory of intelligence, the Cattell Horn Carroll (CHC) Theory (Schneider & McGrew,
112	2018) was ﬁrst introduced at the NFL Scouting Combine in 2012. Bowman et al. (2020)
113	revealed statistically signiﬁcant correlations and multiple regression predictions be-
114	tween the AIQ’s four factor scores and NFL metrics (e.g., Weighted Career Ap-
115	proximate Value (CAV) and Rushing Yards per game). Further, in a current study, NFL
116	quarterbacks with higher AIQ scores threw for more touchdowns and passing yards and
117	had higher quarterback ratings (QBR) and CAV (Boone, 2024). The AIQ has also
118	shown utility in differentiating players in the National Basketball Association (NBA)
119	from those in leagues that are presumed to include less skilled players (e.g., the G
120	League or International Leagues) (Hogan et al., 2023), with signiﬁcant correlations
121	between AIQ factor scores and speciﬁc basketball game statistics (e.g., Player Efﬁ-
122	ciency Rating (PER), Effective Field Goal Percentage (eFG), and Turnovers). AIQ
123	scores have also been signiﬁcantly related to performance statistics in professional
124	baseball (Bowman et al., 2021).
125	   In the initial NFL research on the AIQ (Bowman et al., 2020), investigators analyzed
126	relationships between AIQ scores and position-speciﬁc game data for offensive and
127	defensive players, but did not include offensive linemen (viz., left tackles, left guards,
128	centers, right guards, and right tackles) in those analyses. While offensive linemen may
129	be less well known to fans than other NFL players, they are critical to a team’s success,
130	because they provide offensive players the necessary protection and time to execute
131	winning plays (Krywaruczenko, 2019). In fact, added time for quarterback decision-
132	making has been signiﬁcantly correlated with pass completions (Alamar & Weinstein-
133	Gould, 2008). In addition to pass-blocking, offensive linemen are engaged in essential
134	run-blocking for critical yardage gains. Monson (2023) reported that Pro Football
135	Focus ranked the offensive lines for the two 2023 Super Bowl teams (Philadelphia
136	Eagles and Kansas City Chiefs) 1st and 3rd best in the league, respectively.
137	   A challenge in quantifying game performance of offensive linemen is that objective
138	statistics are minimal; thus the number of penalties committed is a rare quantiﬁable
139	 4                                                           Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
140	
141	performance statistic for this position group. According to NFLpenalties.com, the most
142	frequent penalties committed by offensive linemen in 2020 (45% of all their penalties)
143	were false starts. The NFL Rule Book, Rule 7, Section 4, Article 2, deﬁnes a false start
144	as “any quick abrupt movement by a single offensive player, or by several offensive
145	players in unison, which simulates the start of the snap.” The penalty for a false start is a
146	loss of ﬁve yards from the line of scrimmage and a replay of the down. Clearly, these
147	errors make it harder for an offensive team to obtain a ﬁrst down, impacting the
148	momentum of a drive and sometimes changing the course of a game. For example,
149	Burke (2010) calculated that Alex Barron’s 43 career false start penalties cost his team
150	24.4 potential points over the course of his career, or the equivalent of ﬁve points per
151	season, leading in turn to a cost of 0.62 wins, or about 0.12 wins per season.
152	   While an offensive line works as a single unit with interdependency in their play
153	(Bradbury, 2008; Carroll, et al., 1988), if Player A incurs a false start in a game, it is safe
154	to conclude that Player A is individually at fault for the infraction. Thus, this metric
155	provides a limited but meaningful indication of a player’s individual performance at a
156	position that is difﬁcult to evaluate. Although centers are critical members of the
157	offensive line, they are not often called for false starts because they are the ones who
158	hike the ball, rather than having to react immediately to someone else hiking it. Given
159	the guards’ closer proximity to the center and quarterback, it is logical that they would
160	incur fewer false starts than tackles. In fact, according to NFLpenalties.com, eight of the
161	most penalized offensive linemen for false starts in 2023 were tackles, while two were
162	guards.
163	   For the purposes of this study, false starts may be considered indications of im-
164	pulsivity or loss of focus that may relate to cognitive abilities associated with vigilance
165	and response inhibition. In previous research, self-reported levels of impulsivity have
166	signiﬁcantly predicted sport behaviors like unsportsmanlike conduct (Kang, Kim, &
167	Lee, 2021). Moreover, in a study of handball players, demonstrated levels of im-
168	pulsivity on neurocognitive assessments were positively correlated with technical faults
169	and fouls (Lage et al., 2011). Such research provides a clear rationale for why offensive
170	linemen who are less vigilant/more impulsive would likely commit more false starts per
171	game than other players.
172	   In the context of prior research, literature and logic, we investigated the relationships
173	between neurocognitive tests of impulsivity and vigilance within the AIQ and NFL
174	game-based false start penalties committed by offensive linemen. The AIQ has es-
175	tablished reliability and has been empirically validated as a measure of sport speciﬁc
176	cognitive abilities (Bowman et al., 2020, 2021; Hogan et al., 2023), but it has not been
177	applied to offensive linemen to date. Although the AIQ is a broad cognitive measure,
178	we focused on only two indices of speciﬁc relevance to false start penalties: Simple
179	Reaction Time and Choice Reaction Time. These two measures on the AIQ provide
180	both speed-based scores as well as separate accuracy scores, with the latter denoting a
181	player’s vigilance/impulsivity.
182	 Bowman et al.                                                                                5
183	
184	Hypotheses
185	First, based on patterns observed in the NFL, we hypothesized that, within our sample,
186	tackles would have a higher rate of false start penalties per game than guards. Next,
187	given the results of previous research on measures of abilities identiﬁed in CHC Theory,
188	we hypothesized a relationship between Reaction Time Task accuracy measures and the
189	number of false starts per game in the NFL. Additionally, we hypothesized that these
190	two AIQ scores would explain a statistically signiﬁcant increase, beyond draft pick and
191	position, in the variance in false starts per game. Draft pick was chosen as the ﬁrst
192	independent variable covariate because the athlete’s pick in the draft represents the
193	player’s estimated value based on the combination of multiple factors (e.g., strength,
194	speed, size, scouting reports, personality, etc.). Player position was chosen as the
195	second covariate, given the hypothesized pattern of false starts per game for offensive
196	linemen. Ultimately, he AIQ should be able to improve predictive power beyond these
197	variables if it is to provide utility. Thus, the following hypotheses were proposed:
198	H1: There will be a signiﬁcant difference in false start penalties per game between
199	tackles and guards.
200	H2: The two AIQ reaction time indices of vigilance and impulse control will be
201	signiﬁcantly correlated with false start penalties per game for offensive linemen. More
202	speciﬁcally, the number of commission errors on the simple RT task will be positively
203	related to false starts and accuracy on the Choice RT task will be negatively related to
204	false starts.
205	H3: The two AIQ indices of vigilance and impulse control will provide a statistically
206	signiﬁcant increase in the explanation of variance in false starts per game, beyond draft
207	pick and position.
208	
209	
210	
211	Method
212	Participants
213	We administered the AIQ to 315 offensive linemen between 2014 and 2021, prior to
214	their respective NFL Draft year. From these offensive linemen, we purposely excluded
215	centers because, as hikers of the ball, they are far less susceptible to false start penalties.
216	Among our 315 participants, 85 had played in at least 17 games by the end of the
217	2021 NFL season, which is equivalent to one full NFL season. This level of partic-
218	ipation was considered the minimum threshold for inclusion in these analyses.
219	
220	
221	Ethical Considerations
222	Participation in the study was voluntary, and we obtained informed consent for this
223	research from all participants in accordance with the NFL draft evaluation procedures.
224	Additionally, only anonymized data were accessed and used for this study. Due to fact
225	 6                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
226	
227	that the data were anonymized and archival, this study was determined to have exempt
228	status by an Institutional Review Board.
229	
230	
231	Assessment Instrument
232	Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ). The Athletic Intelligence Test is a comprehensive
233	measure of cognitive ability composed of 10 subtests. It is administered on a tablet by a
234	software program. Subtests are presented in a ﬁxed, successive order, with audio/visual
235	instructions provided before the start of each task. The administration time for the AIQ
236	generally ranges from 35–38 minutes. See Bowman et al. (2020) or Hogan et al. (2023)
237	for additional information about each subtest and factor.
238	    We analyzed results from two subtests on the AIQ. Both measures assess Reaction
239	Time, which has been deﬁned as the ability to react and/or make decisions quickly in
240	response to simple stimuli (Flanagan et al., 2006). These abilities are typically
241	measured by chronometric measures of reaction time. The AIQ includes a measure of
242	Simple Reaction Time and Choice Reaction Time. Simple Reaction Time is the latency
243	period (in milliseconds) of a response to a single stimulus (visual or auditory) presented
244	at a particular point of time. By contrast, Choice Reaction Time requires the accurate
245	and immediate processing of target stimuli among a series of two or more distractor
246	stimuli, depending on which is signaled.
247	    On the AIQ, both subtests yield scores based on the average reaction time for each
248	trial, and separate scores that are derived based on the accuracy of the respondent. For
249	the simple reaction time task, accuracy is best evaluated with number of commission
250	errors or false alarms. For the choice reaction time task, the best measures is the d prime
251	statistic, an indicator of sensitivity or discriminability. It is calculated based on the
252	number of correct hits (pressing the button when the target appeared) and the number of
253	commission errors (pressing the button prematurely, when a target has not appeared).
254	Thus, these reaction time accuracy scores are not based on the speed of an individual’s
255	response but rather on their ability to remain vigilant and inhibit impulses.
256	    Given the factors that likely affect a player’s propensity to commit false start
257	penalties, we postulated that their reaction time accuracy scores rather than speed-based
258	(reaction time) scores or other cognitive ability scores would be most impactful. As
259	offensive linemen get into position, they are essentially waiting for a signal. They must
260	engage in the play as soon as possible after the ball is hiked. Reacting before the ball is
261	hiked is a penalty; reacting late means your advantage in the play is lost. The most basic
262	aspects of this play would appear to be like that of a Simple RT task. However, there are
263	numerous distractors including the movements of the defense, movement in the
264	backﬁeld, fan noise, and a hard count from the quarterback, while the lineman must
265	only attend to the correct cue, the action of the center. If they react to one of the
266	distractors, they will incur a false start penalty. The cognitive requirements of this game
267	situation appear related to the vigilance/impulse control required in the Choice
268	RT Task.
269	 Bowman et al.                                                                         7
270	
271	Procedure
272	Trained administrators brieﬂy described the assessment protocol before asking par-
273	ticipants to provide informed consent, which included their express right to discontinue
274	responding to assessment questions at any time. When the athletes arrived at the
275	evaluation room, the administrator led them to the testing station and brieﬂy explained
276	the testing procedures. Next, the administrator initiated the computer program for the
277	participants and presented them with headphones for audio instructions.
278	
279	
280	Data Analysis
281	We conducted all statistical analyses using the Statistical Package for the Social
282	Sciences (SPSS 29.0; IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA), and we considered a p-value of <
283	.05 as statistically signiﬁcant. Power analyses using the G*Power program (Faul et al.,
284	2007) demonstrated that we had 80% power for detecting large effect sizes in all our
285	planned analyses. We computed descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations)
286	for all outcome measures. Additionally, we accounted for games played by calculating
287	the number of False starts per Game (FSG), our primary dependent variable. For the
288	AIQ measures, we focused on the commission errors for the simple RT and calculated
289	d’ for choice RT, as described by Macmillan and Creelman (1991; see also Stanislaw &
290	Todorov 1999). We used a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test for dif-
291	ferences between position (Guard, Tackle, and Both) on number of False Starts per
292	Game, utilizing the REGWQ post hoc test. We used hierarchical regression to test the
293	effects of draft pick1, position, commission errors for simple RT, and d’ for choice RT
294	on number of False Starts per game. This same analysis also included the calculation of
295	the zero-order correlations between False Starts per Game and the predictor variables.
296	
297	
298	Results
299	Our ﬁrst hypothesis required a determination of whether the player’s false starts in NFL
300	games were related to their position on the ﬁeld, with the expectation that there would
301	be false start differences between players in tackle vs. guard positions. We ran a one-
302	way between subjects ANOVA which demonstrated a signiﬁcant difference between
303	three groups (i.e., tackles, guards, and players who played both tackle and guard) F

366	
367	Discussion
368	In recent years, mounting research has highlighted relationships among cognitive
369	factors and performance in professional sports (Jacobson & Matthaeus, 2014; Voss
370	et al., 2010). With physical traits and abilities and personality variables already being
371	measured in granular detail, it makes sense that teams across all sports would begin to
372	assess cognitive abilities in a similar way, to obtain incremental advantages in player
373	selection and development. Beyond various tasks used in past cognitive research, the
374	Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ), appears to hold particular promise as a reliable
375	and valid comprehensive cognitive assessment tool with implications across a range of
376	professional sports (Bowman et al., 2020, 2021; Hogan et al., 2023).
377	   In the current study, we applied a similar research methodology as prior investigators
378	who correlated AIQ results with speciﬁc game performance, except that we studied an
379	unheralded position group in American football, offensive linemen. Given the chal-
380	lenges of assessing the individual game performance of offensive linemen, we focused
381	on the objective dependent variable of their number of false start penalties, which
382	negatively impact the offensive team’s goal of moving the ball into the opponent’s end
383	zone (Krywaruczenko, 2019).
384	   In line with our ﬁrst hypothesis, we found a signiﬁcant difference among the number
385	of false starts for players who played different positions on the offensive line. Spe-
386	ciﬁcally, tackles incurred signiﬁcantly more false start penalties per game than guards
387	or players who played both tackle and guard. This is consistent with the pattern of the
388	most penalized offensive linemen in the NFL last year, and makes intuitive sense, as
389	tackles are farther away from the center, and therefore, may be less able to discriminate
390	cues for the ball being hiked. There may also be some parallel to research on Pieron’s
391	Law on perceptual decision-making, which indicates that mean response times decrease
392	(and response accuracy increases) as stimulus intensity increases (van Maanen et al.,
393	2021). Speciﬁcally, closer proximity to the source (i.e., center hiking the ball) may
394	represent greater stimulus intensity.
395	   Consistent with our second hypothesis, players’ levels of vigilance and impulsivity
396	were signiﬁcantly correlated with the number of false start penalties they incurred per
397	game. In the Simple Reaction Time Task, the greater number of commission errors was
398	positively related to the greater number of FSPG. Additionally, as hypothesized, the
399	measure of accuracy for the Choice Reaction Time task was signiﬁcantly negatively
400	correlated with FSPG and provided a statistically signiﬁcant increase in explained
401	variance in FSPG beyond draft pick and position (i.e., Hypothesis 3).
402	   Interestingly, while this relationship emerged for Simple Reaction Time accuracy, it
403	was not a unique predictor when this variable was entered into the regression model
404	with Draft Pick, position, and d’ for CRT. However, if an offensive lineman struggles
405	 10                                                        Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
406	
407	with impulsivity/vigilance during the more complex Choice Reaction Time test sce-
408	narios, they are at greater risk of committing false start penalties, and this is a unique
409	contributor to the overall model, above and beyond the effect of draft pick and position.
410	Again, this makes intuitive sense, given that the presence of multiple distracting game
411	factors (e.g., hard count from the quarterback, movement from a defender suggesting a
412	potential blitz) may affect a player’s ability to react immediately, but not prematurely to
413	the hiking of the ball.
414	    Overall, our ﬁndings add to a growing body of research underscoring the importance
415	of cognitive factors in sports and the utility of measuring speciﬁc cognitive abilities that
416	have relevance for game performance. Although there are implications in terms of
417	scouting and talent selection, player development and peak performance may be the
418	most critical applications of knowledge gained from applying cognitive assessment in
419	sports. If team representatives and players can understand the unique cognitive
420	strengths needed from players in each position, teams may determine how to set players
421	up for success by matching players’ cognitive proﬁles with given positions, schemes,
422	and strategies, and players may learn what skills are most important to develop. For
423	instance, a wide receiver with weaknesses in visual spatial processing may do better
424	with simpler route trees (e.g., “go route,” etc.). Similarly, an offensive lineman who
425	struggles with impulsivity may perform better when closer to the ball (i.e., playing
426	guard) to be more in rhythm with the count and snap than if farther away (i.e., playing
427	tackle).
428	    Further, when teams and players understand their cognitive strengths and weak-
429	nesses, they can implement drills and strategies tailored to their needs. For example, an
430	offensive lineman who struggles with vigilance/impulse control at the line of scrim-
431	mage, may need to spend extra time in practice working on his “get off” to various
432	counts/cadences from the QB. Coaches may also incorporate noise or other forms of
433	distraction to simulate some of the real challenges of game scenarios. Ultimately, by
434	identifying these individual factors pre-draft, teams may be able to identify and address
435	potential concerns earlier in the player development process. Conversely, if coaches
436	and team personnel lack this kind of information ahead of time, they may experience
437	signiﬁcant frustration by having to acquire it more slowly.
438	
439	Limitations and Directions for Further Research
440	With respect to limitations, the metric we used of false start penalties clearly does not
441	fully assess the complexity of offensive line play. As such, we recommend that in-
442	vestigators identify additional factors, such as individual player rankings (e.g., Pro
443	Football Focus) in future research. Future researchers should also allow for the in-
444	clusion of centers, since centers also play an important role on the offensive line. The
445	inclusion of additional measures of vigilance/impulsivity or other cognitive abilities
446	would also allow comparisons of which tasks are most sensitive to aspects of offensive
447	line play in the NFL. American footbal has several distractors that can lead to increased
448	RT or even false start penalties during the game. A CRT controlled situation is a
449	 Bowman et al.                                                                                   11
450	
451	possibility that can lead to increased preparation time for the response and wrong
452	choice, and the results can give some insights about distractors in the game. Further,
453	researchers might obtain a clearer understanding of the variance in NFL false starts
454	explained by cognitive factors by controlling for the number of false starts incurred
455	during players’ college football careers.
456	   Even in terms of penalties, there are other common infractions on the offensive line,
457	such as holding penalties, that may correlate signiﬁcantly with cognitive factors.
458	Additionally, to address the player development implications noted above, researchers
459	could explore the efﬁcacy of different coaching strategies on penalties incurred for
460	offensive linemen who struggle with vigilance/impulse control. Follow-up research
461	might also address the defensive side of football, perhaps involving a similar penalty to
462	false starts, known as an encroachment, deﬁned by when “a defensive player enters the
463	neutral zone and contacts an offensive player or the ball prior to the snap, or interferes
464	with the ball during the snap…” (National Football League, 2022).
465	
466	
467	
468	Conclusion
469	In the end, though the unique contributions of measures of impulsivity and vigilance
470	appear to be modest in the prediction of false start penalties for offensive linemen, our
471	study provides further support for the role of cognitive assessment in professional
472	sports and serves as an example of how research of this kind can ﬁll important gaps in
473	our understanding of optimal player characteristics. Practically, this information has
474	immediate beneﬁt for tailored coaching and player development strategies.

False Start Penalties of
Offensive Linemen in the
National Football League
(NFL)


James K. Bowman1 , Daniel Krywaruczenko2,
Brandon G. De Flon3, and R. Thomas Boone4



Abstract
Each year in the United States, many factors are considered in the National Football
League’s draft process, including scouting reports, interviews, medical tests, and
measures of players’ strength, speed, anthropometry, and personality. Recently, an
increased emphasis has been placed on players’ psychometrically measured cognitive
abilities. Historically, offensive linemen have been excluded from NFL research, since
they do not have individual performance statistics. In this study, we attempted to ﬁll
that research gap by investigating correlates of offensive linemen’s measured vigilance/
impulsivity. We obtained archival player data from 85 offensive linemen in the years
from 2014–2021 prior to each of these players’ NFL draft. We then used false start
penalties per game (FSPG) as an index of their vigilance/impulsivity (and general
success) on the ﬁeld, and we related those values to Reaction Time tests through
hierarchical multiple regression analyses. After controlling for draft placement, these
players’ higher accuracy on a Choice Reaction Time task accounted for a statistically

the practical utility for player development of these and other cognitive assessments
now used in the NFL.


Keywords
cognition in sport, american football, nﬂ draft, reaction time



Introduction
At the start of the 2023 American football season, the aggregate value of the National
Football League (NFL) was estimated at $163 billion, with the value of the average
team placed at $5.1 billion (Ozanian & Teitelbaum, 2023). In the context of these major
economic pressures, all 32 NFL teams go to great lengths each year to compete for a
championship, including each team’s heavy investment in predicting and improving
individual player’s athletic performance.
   The annual talent identiﬁcation process for players entering the NFL draft includes a
review of the players’ anthropometric measurements and physical attributes (e.g.,
statistics related to their size, strength, and speed) and measures of their psychological
functioning, including both their cognitive abilities and personality functioning. The
development, measurement quality, and practical utility of both these physical and
psychological measures have important limitations. For instance, research to date has
shown inconsistent relationships between player performance on isolated physical tests
and their subsequent NFL game performance (Lyons et al., 2011). Similarly, per-
sonality assessments have limitations, including a self-report bias that can contribute to
inaccurate personality assessment (Roth et al., 1986). Additionally, since longitudinal
research has shown that changes in personality tend to correlate with changes in life
satisfaction, work environment, and socioeconomic status over time (Boyce et al.,
2012; Le et al., 2014), an athlete whose personal wealth is changed dramatically by a
multi-million-dollar NFL contract can experience major changes from initial per-
sonality ﬁndings.
   Perhaps the domain with the greatest research advancements in recent years is
cognitive functioning. Considerable research over 40+ years has shown relationships
between cognitive functioning and athletic performance (Farrow et al., 1998; Faubert,
2013; Vaeyens et al., 2008). For instance, Jacobson and Matthaeus (2014) found that
athletes scored signiﬁcantly higher on measures of inhibition and problem-solving than
non-athletes, and, in a meta-analysis conducted by Voss et al. (2010), athletes scored
higher than non-athletes on measures of processing speed and varied cognitive at-
tention tasks. Some researchers and theorists have argued that the cognitive domain
may be the most important distinguishing factor between elite and non-elite athletes
(Zaichkowsky & Peterson, 2018). Yet, for decades, the Wonderlic Personnel Test was
the sole NFL measure of intellectual ability (Wonderlic, 2013), even while its scores
 Bowman et al.                                                                           3

have not shown predictive validity with respect to NFL player performance (Kuzmits &
Adams, 2008; Lyons et al., 2009). This seemingly led to the NFL’s 2022 announcement
that the Wonderlic Personnel Test would no longer be administered to all prospective
players at the NFL Scouting Combine (O’Connell, 2022).
   Among new cognitive tests developed for use with prospective NFL players, the
Player Assessment Test (PAT; Siena Consulting, 2013) was designed to measure
learning styles, decision-making skills, core intellect, and the ability to respond to
unexpected stimuli (Breer, 2013; Howard, 2013). Unfortunately, despite the 10-year
history of the PAT, there are no peer-reviewed research studies that have identiﬁed
signiﬁcant relationships between scores on factors of the PAT and aspects of NFL game
performance. Other, newer cognitive measures (e.g., APTUS, S2) also lack published
empirical support for NFL applications.
   The one cognitive assessment tool with demonstrated signiﬁcant relationships
between test scores and NFL performance is the Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ;
Bowman et al., 2020; Boone, 2024). The AIQ, based on the most empirically supported
theory of intelligence, the Cattell Horn Carroll (CHC) Theory (Schneider & McGrew,
2018) was ﬁrst introduced at the NFL Scouting Combine in 2012. Bowman et al. (2020)
revealed statistically signiﬁcant correlations and multiple regression predictions be-
tween the AIQ’s four factor scores and NFL metrics (e.g., Weighted Career Ap-
proximate Value (CAV) and Rushing Yards per game). Further, in a current study, NFL
quarterbacks with higher AIQ scores threw for more touchdowns and passing yards and
had higher quarterback ratings (QBR) and CAV (Boone, 2024). The AIQ has also
shown utility in differentiating players in the National Basketball Association (NBA)
from those in leagues that are presumed to include less skilled players (e.g., the G
League or International Leagues) (Hogan et al., 2023), with signiﬁcant correlations
between AIQ factor scores and speciﬁc basketball game statistics (e.g., Player Efﬁ-
ciency Rating (PER), Effective Field Goal Percentage (eFG), and Turnovers). AIQ
scores have also been signiﬁcantly related to performance statistics in professional
baseball (Bowman et al., 2021).
   In the initial NFL research on the AIQ (Bowman et al., 2020), investigators analyzed
relationships between AIQ scores and position-speciﬁc game data for offensive and
defensive players, but did not include offensive linemen (viz., left tackles, left guards,
centers, right guards, and right tackles) in those analyses. While offensive linemen may
be less well known to fans than other NFL players, they are critical to a team’s success,
because they provide offensive players the necessary protection and time to execute
winning plays (Krywaruczenko, 2019). In fact, added time for quarterback decision-
making has been signiﬁcantly correlated with pass completions (Alamar & Weinstein-
Gould, 2008). In addition to pass-blocking, offensive linemen are engaged in essential
run-blocking for critical yardage gains. Monson (2023) reported that Pro Football
Focus ranked the offensive lines for the two 2023 Super Bowl teams (Philadelphia
Eagles and Kansas City Chiefs) 1st and 3rd best in the league, respectively.
   A challenge in quantifying game performance of offensive linemen is that objective
statistics are minimal; thus the number of penalties committed is a rare quantiﬁable

performance statistic for this position group. According to NFLpenalties.com, the most
frequent penalties committed by offensive linemen in 2020 (45% of all their penalties)
were false starts. The NFL Rule Book, Rule 7, Section 4, Article 2, deﬁnes a false start
as “any quick abrupt movement by a single offensive player, or by several offensive
players in unison, which simulates the start of the snap.” The penalty for a false start is a
loss of ﬁve yards from the line of scrimmage and a replay of the down. Clearly, these
errors make it harder for an offensive team to obtain a ﬁrst down, impacting the
momentum of a drive and sometimes changing the course of a game. For example,
Burke (2010) calculated that Alex Barron’s 43 career false start penalties cost his team
24.4 potential points over the course of his career, or the equivalent of ﬁve points per
season, leading in turn to a cost of 0.62 wins, or about 0.12 wins per season.
   While an offensive line works as a single unit with interdependency in their play
(Bradbury, 2008; Carroll, et al., 1988), if Player A incurs a false start in a game, it is safe
to conclude that Player A is individually at fault for the infraction. Thus, this metric
provides a limited but meaningful indication of a player’s individual performance at a
position that is difﬁcult to evaluate. Although centers are critical members of the
offensive line, they are not often called for false starts because they are the ones who
hike the ball, rather than having to react immediately to someone else hiking it. Given
the guards’ closer proximity to the center and quarterback, it is logical that they would
incur fewer false starts than tackles. In fact, according to NFLpenalties.com, eight of the
most penalized offensive linemen for false starts in 2023 were tackles, while two were
guards.
   For the purposes of this study, false starts may be considered indications of im-
pulsivity or loss of focus that may relate to cognitive abilities associated with vigilance
and response inhibition. In previous research, self-reported levels of impulsivity have
signiﬁcantly predicted sport behaviors like unsportsmanlike conduct (Kang, Kim, &
Lee, 2021). Moreover, in a study of handball players, demonstrated levels of im-
pulsivity on neurocognitive assessments were positively correlated with technical faults
and fouls (Lage et al., 2011). Such research provides a clear rationale for why offensive
linemen who are less vigilant/more impulsive would likely commit more false starts per
game than other players.
   In the context of prior research, literature and logic, we investigated the relationships
between neurocognitive tests of impulsivity and vigilance within the AIQ and NFL
game-based false start penalties committed by offensive linemen. The AIQ has es-
tablished reliability and has been empirically validated as a measure of sport speciﬁc
cognitive abilities (Bowman et al., 2020, 2021; Hogan et al., 2023), but it has not been
applied to offensive linemen to date. Although the AIQ is a broad cognitive measure,
we focused on only two indices of speciﬁc relevance to false start penalties: Simple
Reaction Time and Choice Reaction Time. These two measures on the AIQ provide
both speed-based scores as well as separate accuracy scores, with the latter denoting a
player’s vigilance/impulsivity.

Hypotheses
First, based on patterns observed in the NFL, we hypothesized that, within our sample,
tackles would have a higher rate of false start penalties per game than guards. Next,
given the results of previous research on measures of abilities identiﬁed in CHC Theory,
we hypothesized a relationship between Reaction Time Task accuracy measures and the
number of false starts per game in the NFL. Additionally, we hypothesized that these
two AIQ scores would explain a statistically signiﬁcant increase, beyond draft pick and
position, in the variance in false starts per game. Draft pick was chosen as the ﬁrst
independent variable covariate because the athlete’s pick in the draft represents the
player’s estimated value based on the combination of multiple factors (e.g., strength,
speed, size, scouting reports, personality, etc.). Player position was chosen as the
second covariate, given the hypothesized pattern of false starts per game for offensive
linemen. Ultimately, he AIQ should be able to improve predictive power beyond these
variables if it is to provide utility. Thus, the following hypotheses were proposed:
H1: There will be a signiﬁcant difference in false start penalties per game between
tackles and guards.
H2: The two AIQ reaction time indices of vigilance and impulse control will be
signiﬁcantly correlated with false start penalties per game for offensive linemen. More
speciﬁcally, the number of commission errors on the simple RT task will be positively
related to false starts and accuracy on the Choice RT task will be negatively related to
false starts.
H3: The two AIQ indices of vigilance and impulse control will provide a statistically
signiﬁcant increase in the explanation of variance in false starts per game, beyond draft
pick and position.



Method
Participants
We administered the AIQ to 315 offensive linemen between 2014 and 2021, prior to
their respective NFL Draft year. From these offensive linemen, we purposely excluded
centers because, as hikers of the ball, they are far less susceptible to false start penalties.
Among our 315 participants, 85 had played in at least 17 games by the end of the
2021 NFL season, which is equivalent to one full NFL season. This level of partic-
ipation was considered the minimum threshold for inclusion in these analyses.


Ethical Considerations
Participation in the study was voluntary, and we obtained informed consent for this
research from all participants in accordance with the NFL draft evaluation procedures.
Additionally, only anonymized data were accessed and used for this study. Due to fact

that the data were anonymized and archival, this study was determined to have exempt
status by an Institutional Review Board.


Assessment Instrument
Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ). The Athletic Intelligence Test is a comprehensive
measure of cognitive ability composed of 10 subtests. It is administered on a tablet by a
software program. Subtests are presented in a ﬁxed, successive order, with audio/visual
instructions provided before the start of each task. The administration time for the AIQ
generally ranges from 35–38 minutes. See Bowman et al. (2020) or Hogan et al. (2023)
for additional information about each subtest and factor.
    We analyzed results from two subtests on the AIQ. Both measures assess Reaction
Time, which has been deﬁned as the ability to react and/or make decisions quickly in
response to simple stimuli (Flanagan et al., 2006). These abilities are typically
measured by chronometric measures of reaction time. The AIQ includes a measure of
Simple Reaction Time and Choice Reaction Time. Simple Reaction Time is the latency
period (in milliseconds) of a response to a single stimulus (visual or auditory) presented
at a particular point of time. By contrast, Choice Reaction Time requires the accurate
and immediate processing of target stimuli among a series of two or more distractor
stimuli, depending on which is signaled.
    On the AIQ, both subtests yield scores based on the average reaction time for each
trial, and separate scores that are derived based on the accuracy of the respondent. For
the simple reaction time task, accuracy is best evaluated with number of commission
errors or false alarms. For the choice reaction time task, the best measures is the d prime
statistic, an indicator of sensitivity or discriminability. It is calculated based on the
number of correct hits (pressing the button when the target appeared) and the number of
commission errors (pressing the button prematurely, when a target has not appeared).
Thus, these reaction time accuracy scores are not based on the speed of an individual’s
response but rather on their ability to remain vigilant and inhibit impulses.
    Given the factors that likely affect a player’s propensity to commit false start
penalties, we postulated that their reaction time accuracy scores rather than speed-based
(reaction time) scores or other cognitive ability scores would be most impactful. As
offensive linemen get into position, they are essentially waiting for a signal. They must
engage in the play as soon as possible after the ball is hiked. Reacting before the ball is
hiked is a penalty; reacting late means your advantage in the play is lost. The most basic
aspects of this play would appear to be like that of a Simple RT task. However, there are
numerous distractors including the movements of the defense, movement in the
backﬁeld, fan noise, and a hard count from the quarterback, while the lineman must
only attend to the correct cue, the action of the center. If they react to one of the
distractors, they will incur a false start penalty. The cognitive requirements of this game
situation appear related to the vigilance/impulse control required in the Choice
RT Task.

Procedure
Trained administrators brieﬂy described the assessment protocol before asking par-
ticipants to provide informed consent, which included their express right to discontinue
responding to assessment questions at any time. When the athletes arrived at the
evaluation room, the administrator led them to the testing station and brieﬂy explained
the testing procedures. Next, the administrator initiated the computer program for the
participants and presented them with headphones for audio instructions.


Data Analysis
We conducted all statistical analyses using the Statistical Package for the Social
Sciences (SPSS 29.0; IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA), and we considered a p-value of <
.05 as statistically signiﬁcant. Power analyses using the G*Power program (Faul et al.,
2007) demonstrated that we had 80% power for detecting large effect sizes in all our
planned analyses. We computed descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations)
for all outcome measures. Additionally, we accounted for games played by calculating
the number of False starts per Game (FSG), our primary dependent variable. For the
AIQ measures, we focused on the commission errors for the simple RT and calculated
d’ for choice RT, as described by Macmillan and Creelman (1991; see also Stanislaw &
Todorov 1999). We used a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test for dif-
ferences between position (Guard, Tackle, and Both) on number of False Starts per
Game, utilizing the REGWQ post hoc test. We used hierarchical regression to test the
effects of draft pick1, position, commission errors for simple RT, and d’ for choice RT
on number of False Starts per game. This same analysis also included the calculation of
the zero-order correlations between False Starts per Game and the predictor variables.

games were related to their position on the ﬁeld, with the expectation that there would
be false start differences between players in tackle vs. guard positions. We ran a one-

three groups (i.e., tackles, guards, and players who played both tackle and guard) F
(2,84) = 3.96, p = .02. A Student-Newman-Keuls post-hoc test revealed that tackles
(n = 36; M = .16, SD = .09) were more likely to have false starts than guards (n = 18,
M = .10, SD = .05) or than players who played both positions (n = 31; M = .12,
SD = 08).

Discussion
In recent years, mounting research has highlighted relationships among cognitive
factors and performance in professional sports (Jacobson & Matthaeus, 2014; Voss
et al., 2010). With physical traits and abilities and personality variables already being
measured in granular detail, it makes sense that teams across all sports would begin to
assess cognitive abilities in a similar way, to obtain incremental advantages in player
selection and development. Beyond various tasks used in past cognitive research, the
Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ), appears to hold particular promise as a reliable
and valid comprehensive cognitive assessment tool with implications across a range of
professional sports (Bowman et al., 2020, 2021; Hogan et al., 2023).
   In the current study, we applied a similar research methodology as prior investigators
who correlated AIQ results with speciﬁc game performance, except that we studied an
unheralded position group in American football, offensive linemen. Given the chal-
lenges of assessing the individual game performance of offensive linemen, we focused
on the objective dependent variable of their number of false start penalties, which
negatively impact the offensive team’s goal of moving the ball into the opponent’s end
zone (Krywaruczenko, 2019).
   In line with our ﬁrst hypothesis, we found a signiﬁcant difference among the number
of false starts for players who played different positions on the offensive line. Spe-
ciﬁcally, tackles incurred signiﬁcantly more false start penalties per game than guards
or players who played both tackle and guard. This is consistent with the pattern of the
most penalized offensive linemen in the NFL last year, and makes intuitive sense, as
tackles are farther away from the center, and therefore, may be less able to discriminate
cues for the ball being hiked. There may also be some parallel to research on Pieron’s
Law on perceptual decision-making, which indicates that mean response times decrease
(and response accuracy increases) as stimulus intensity increases (van Maanen et al.,
2021). Speciﬁcally, closer proximity to the source (i.e., center hiking the ball) may
represent greater stimulus intensity.
   Consistent with our second hypothesis, players’ levels of vigilance and impulsivity
were signiﬁcantly correlated with the number of false start penalties they incurred per
game. In the Simple Reaction Time Task, the greater number of commission errors was
positively related to the greater number of FSPG. Additionally, as hypothesized, the
measure of accuracy for the Choice Reaction Time task was signiﬁcantly negatively
correlated with FSPG and provided a statistically signiﬁcant increase in explained
variance in FSPG beyond draft pick and position (i.e., Hypothesis 3).
   Interestingly, while this relationship emerged for Simple Reaction Time accuracy, it
was not a unique predictor when this variable was entered into the regression model
with Draft Pick, position, and d’ for CRT. However, if an offensive lineman struggles

with impulsivity/vigilance during the more complex Choice Reaction Time test sce-
narios, they are at greater risk of committing false start penalties, and this is a unique
contributor to the overall model, above and beyond the effect of draft pick and position.
Again, this makes intuitive sense, given that the presence of multiple distracting game
factors (e.g., hard count from the quarterback, movement from a defender suggesting a
potential blitz) may affect a player’s ability to react immediately, but not prematurely to
the hiking of the ball.
    Overall, our ﬁndings add to a growing body of research underscoring the importance
of cognitive factors in sports and the utility of measuring speciﬁc cognitive abilities that
have relevance for game performance. Although there are implications in terms of
scouting and talent selection, player development and peak performance may be the
most critical applications of knowledge gained from applying cognitive assessment in
sports. If team representatives and players can understand the unique cognitive
strengths needed from players in each position, teams may determine how to set players
up for success by matching players’ cognitive proﬁles with given positions, schemes,
and strategies, and players may learn what skills are most important to develop. For
instance, a wide receiver with weaknesses in visual spatial processing may do better
with simpler route trees (e.g., “go route,” etc.). Similarly, an offensive lineman who
struggles with impulsivity may perform better when closer to the ball (i.e., playing
guard) to be more in rhythm with the count and snap than if farther away (i.e., playing
tackle).
    Further, when teams and players understand their cognitive strengths and weak-
nesses, they can implement drills and strategies tailored to their needs. For example, an
offensive lineman who struggles with vigilance/impulse control at the line of scrim-
mage, may need to spend extra time in practice working on his “get off” to various
counts/cadences from the QB. Coaches may also incorporate noise or other forms of
distraction to simulate some of the real challenges of game scenarios. Ultimately, by
identifying these individual factors pre-draft, teams may be able to identify and address
potential concerns earlier in the player development process. Conversely, if coaches
and team personnel lack this kind of information ahead of time, they may experience
signiﬁcant frustration by having to acquire it more slowly.

Limitations and Directions for Further Research
With respect to limitations, the metric we used of false start penalties clearly does not
fully assess the complexity of offensive line play. As such, we recommend that in-
vestigators identify additional factors, such as individual player rankings (e.g., Pro
Football Focus) in future research. Future researchers should also allow for the in-
clusion of centers, since centers also play an important role on the offensive line. The
inclusion of additional measures of vigilance/impulsivity or other cognitive abilities
would also allow comparisons of which tasks are most sensitive to aspects of offensive
line play in the NFL. American footbal has several distractors that can lead to increased
RT or even false start penalties during the game. A CRT controlled situation is a

possibility that can lead to increased preparation time for the response and wrong
choice, and the results can give some insights about distractors in the game. Further,
researchers might obtain a clearer understanding of the variance in NFL false starts
explained by cognitive factors by controlling for the number of false starts incurred
during players’ college football careers.
   Even in terms of penalties, there are other common infractions on the offensive line,
such as holding penalties, that may correlate signiﬁcantly with cognitive factors.
Additionally, to address the player development implications noted above, researchers
could explore the efﬁcacy of different coaching strategies on penalties incurred for
offensive linemen who struggle with vigilance/impulse control. Follow-up research
might also address the defensive side of football, perhaps involving a similar penalty to
false starts, known as an encroachment, deﬁned by when “a defensive player enters the
neutral zone and contacts an offensive player or the ball prior to the snap, or interferes
with the ball during the snap…” (National Football League, 2022).



Conclusion
In the end, though the unique contributions of measures of impulsivity and vigilance
appear to be modest in the prediction of false start penalties for offensive linemen, our
study provides further support for the role of cognitive assessment in professional
sports and serves as an example of how research of this kind can ﬁll important gaps in
our understanding of optimal player characteristics. Practically, this information has
immediate beneﬁt for tailored coaching and player development strategies.

                The Reliability of Individualized Load–Velocity Proﬁles
                         Harry G. Banyard, Kazunori Nosaka, Alex D. Vernon, and G. Gregory Haff

     Purpose: To examine the reliability of peak velocity (PV), mean propulsive velocity (MPV), and mean velocity (MV) in the
     development of load–velocity proﬁles (LVP) in the full-depth free-weight back squat performed with maximal concentric effort.
     Methods: Eighteen resistance-trained men performed a baseline 1-repetition maximum (1-RM) back-squat trial and 3 subsequent
     1-RM trials used for reliability analyses, with 48-h intervals between trials. 1-RM trials comprised lifts from 6 relative loads
     including 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 90%, and 100% 1-RM. Individualized LVPs for PV, MPV, or MV were derived from loads that
     were highly reliable based on the following criteria: intraclass correlation coefﬁcient (ICC) >.70, coefﬁcient of variation
     (CV) ≤10%, and Cohen d effect size (ES) <0.60. Results: PV was highly reliable at all 6 loads. MPV and MV were highly reliable
     at 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 90% but not 100% 1-RM (MPV: ICC = .66, CV = 18.0%, ES = 0.10, SEM = 0.04 m·s−1; MV:
     ICC = .55, CV = 19.4%, ES = 0.08, SEM = 0.04 m·s−1). When considering the reliable ranges, almost perfect correlations were
     observed for LVPs derived from PV20–100% (r = .91–.93), MPV20–90% (r = .92–.94), and MV20–90% (r = .94–.95). Furthermore,
     the LVPs were not signiﬁcantly different (P > .05) between trials or movement velocities or between linear regression versus 2nd-
     order polynomial ﬁts. Conclusions: PV20–100%, MPV20–90%, and MV20–90% are reliable and can be utilized to develop LVPs
     using linear regression. Conceptually, LVPs can be used to monitor changes in movement velocity and employed as a method for
     adjusting sessional training loads according to daily readiness.

     Keywords: peak velocity, mean velocity, mean propulsive velocity, back squat, velocity-based training

PV was highly reliable at all six loads, while MPV and MV were reliable at 20 to 90% but not at 100% 1RM (MPV ICC = .66, CV = 18.0%; MV ICC = .55, CV = 19.4%). Load-velocity profiles built from the reliable loads had almost perfect correlations in the abstract (r = .91 to .93 for PV, .92 to .94 for MPV, .94 to .95 for MV), and linear and second-order polynomial fits did not differ significantly.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 18 resistance-trained men tested on one exercise (free-weight back squat) over three repeat trials, so the reliability estimates cannot be assumed for other lifts, sports, women or other training levels. The study does not test whether the profiles detect fatigue or training change over time.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could assume that any velocity-based profile is reliable, or that the velocities in these profiles will detect fatigue, when the study tested test-retest reliability of back-squat velocities in one lab setting and did not test sensitivity to training or fatigue.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2018,
   "citation": "Banyard HG, Nosaka K, Vernon AD, Haff GG. The Reliability of Individualized Load-Velocity Profiles. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018;13(6):763-769.",
   "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2017-0610",
   "abstract": "This study examined the reliability of peak velocity (PV), mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and mean velocity (MV) for building individual load-velocity profiles (LVPs) in the full-depth free-weight back squat. Eighteen resistance-trained men completed a baseline 1RM and three further 1RM trials 48 h apart, with loads from 20 to 100% 1RM. PV was reliable at all loads, MPV and MV were reliable up to 90% 1RM but not at 100%, and profiles from the reliable loads were highly correlated and did not differ between trials, velocities or fit types. The authors conclude that linear profiles from these reliable loads can be used to monitor velocity and adjust session loads according to daily readiness.",
   "tldr": "In resistance-trained men, bar velocity measured at lighter and moderate loads was reliable enough to build individual load-velocity profiles for the back squat. Velocity at 100% 1RM was not reliable for MPV or MV and should be left out of those profiles.",
   "methods": "Test-retest reliability study. Baseline 1RM back squat, then three 1RM trials 48 h apart, with repetitions at 20, 40, 60, 80, 90 and 100% 1RM. Velocity was measured with four linear position transducers sampled at 1000 Hz. Reliability used ICC, CV, Cohen's d and smallest detectable difference (SDD). Load-velocity profiles were fitted with linear regression and second-order polynomials, and correlations were compared with Fisher's r-to-z transformation.",
   "findings": "PV was highly reliable at all six loads, including 100% 1RM. MPV and MV were highly reliable at 20 to 90% 1RM but not at 100% (MPV ICC = .66, CV = 18.0%, ES = 0.10; MV ICC = .55, CV = 19.4%, ES = 0.08). At 20% 1RM the SDD was 0.17 m/s for PV, 0.08 m/s for MPV and 0.06 m/s for MV. Individual profiles had correlations of r = .89 to .99 (PV), .90 to .99 (MPV) and .90 to .99 (MV). Linear and polynomial fits, the three velocities and the trials did not differ significantly. Group 1RM reliability was high (ICC = .99, CV = 2.0%).",
   "limitations": "Only 18 resistance-trained men, all tested on one exercise, with three trials 48 h apart. Reliability is not tested over longer periods or during training. The stated reliability criteria differ slightly between the Methods (moderate CV of 10% or more) and the abstract (CV of 10% or less), and the abstract's group-level correlation ranges are not shown in the Results, which report individual profile correlations of .89 to .99. The findings apply to free-weight back squats with a set depth and maximal concentric effort. The authors note that results may not transfer to other exercises.",
   "practicalImplications": "Before using load-velocity profiling for back squats, run a 1RM test, build each athlete's own profile from PV at 20 to 100% 1RM or MPV or MV at 20 to 90% 1RM, and fit a linear regression. Keep the velocity at 100% 1RM out of MPV and MV profiles. Change loads only when a velocity falls outside the smallest detectable difference for that measure, and only when bar displacement and maximal concentric effort are kept consistent.",
   "athleteDev": "Individual back-squat profiles built from reliable bar velocities at lighter and moderate loads can help decide whether a velocity drop is real. For example, at 20% 1RM a change of less than 0.06 m/s in MV or less than 0.17 m/s in PV is within measurement error, so it should not drive a load change.",
   "rtp": "The study tested healthy, resistance-trained men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so these profiles cannot be used to judge readiness after injury."
 }
}

   "abstract": "This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the correlations between internal load measures (sRPE, sRPE-TL and TRIMP) and external load measures (total distance, high-speed running distance, accelerometer load and sustained impacts) in team-sport athletes during training and match play. It also examined whether training mode moderates these relationships. Thirteen studies with 295 athletes and 10,418 session observations were included. Internal measures showed consistently positive associations with running and accelerometer-derived external loads, but their size and uncertainty depended on the measure and the training mode. The authors conclude that total running distance had the strongest association with internal load.",
   "tldr": "Across 295 team-sport athletes, session RPE and heart-rate load rose with external load in every case, but how strongly they were linked depended on the measure and the training mode. Session RPE load (sRPE-TL) tracked external load more closely than heart-rate TRIMP, and total running distance was the external measure most strongly linked to internal load.",
   "methods": "Systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL up to September 2017, following PRISMA, with two reviewers screening independently. Eligible studies reported a correlation between an internal and external load measure from team-sport athletes in unstructured training or match play. Studies with youth or injured athletes, experimental trials or non-category RPE scales were excluded. Random-effects meta-analyses (Knapp-Hartung 90% CIs, DerSimonian-Laird tau) were run for each dataset, and random-effects meta-regression examined training mode, with magnitude-based inferences.",
   "findings": "Pooled correlations, all positive, were: sRPE-TL with total distance r = 0.79 (90% CI 0.74 to 0.83), with accelerometer load r = 0.63 (0.54 to 0.70), with impacts r = 0.57 (0.47 to 0.64), and with high-speed distance r = 0.47 (0.32 to 0.59). TRIMP with accelerometer load was r = 0.54 (0.40 to 0.66). sRPE with per-minute external measures ranged from r = 0.22 to 0.29, with unclear inferences. Training mode explained 24% of between-estimate variance for sRPE-TL with high-speed distance, and 100% for sRPE-TL with total distance and accelerometer load, and TRIMP with accelerometer load, in the models with enough estimates.",
   "limitations": "Only data from healthy, non-injured team-sport athletes in normal training or match play were included, so the findings do not cover injured athletes or women. Heterogeneity was large for several relationships. Study designs were unstructured and observational, with varied GPS and accelerometer devices, sampling rates and correlation methods. Some studies pooled repeated sessions as one sample, which may inflate or distort correlations. Several datasets had few estimates, and some relationships could not be inferred. The authors also note possible mathematical coupling, since session duration is part of both internal and external load totals.",
   "practicalImplications": "Monitor session RPE load (sRPE-TL) alongside total distance and accelerometer load, rather than relying on one measure, since the authors found that no single measure captures all training. Avoid external-to-internal load ratios, which the authors say are not valid for most of these relationships, and analyse continuous measures or changes over time instead. Compare sessions within the same training mode, because the links between load measures differ across modes, and consider collecting differential RPE to separate physical from perceptual load.",
   "athleteDev": "Total distance and accelerometer load track session RPE load well in team-sport training, so the two can be read together to judge how hard a session was for players.  }
}

91	                      1. Introduction
92	                            Recovery is a trending topic in the field of sports science [1], and even more so in
93	                      the world of elite sport. This is evidenced by the significant increase [1,2] in scientific
94	                      publications during the last 10 years as teams look to find a competitive edge during
95	                      competitions. Different protocols describe specific recovery methodologies that can be
96	                      employed in order to achieve more efficient recovery processes, these include (1) recovery
97	                      strategies [2,3] —foam roll [4,5], massage [6], compression garments [7,8], stretching [9],
98	                      nutrition [10], active recovery [11], sleep [12], water immersion [13], (2) combinations of
99	                      recovery strategies [14,15], (3) sport-specific recovery characteristics—soccer [16,17], basket-
100	                      ball [18,19], volleyball [20], rugby [21], and combat sports [22], and (4) emerging recovery
101	                      strategies [23]. Additionally, factors, such as recovery time-periods—post-match [16,17]
102	                      and during congested schedules [24], have also been investigated, with emerging literature
103	                      examining recovery specific to female athletes [25] and youth athletes [26,27]. However,
104	                      it is notable that the recovery of coaching and performance staff in elite sports seems
105	                      to have been forgotten. This opinion delineates the elite sports organizational structure
106	                      and specific performance–fatigue characteristics of team staff members and key recovery
107	                      considerations.
108	
109	                      2. Recovery Domains
110	                           Recovery is a complex, multifactorial issue. Collectively, the scientific literature
111	                      reports that the primary aim of recovery methods is to accelerate the biological recovery
112	                      process in shorter time periods [16]. Bird [3] described four essential recovery domains,
113	                      these being neural, muscular, substrate, and psychological (Table 1). Additionally, self-
114	                      perception of perceived recovery is also an important consideration, which may affect the
115	                      balance between happiness and wellness in elite sports athletes [28], especially during
116	                      periods of congested travel and competition. Key observations from research on recovery
117	                      in team sports highlight the fatiguing effect of traveling [29,30] in addition to training
118	                      and competing [31]. As a result, new approaches and practical applications of recovery
119	                      strategies have been discussed to optimize travel and minimize its negative effects on
120	                      health and performance in team sports athletes [32], with little mention of coaching and
121	                      performance staff members [33].

240	                            Regarding team staff members (sports coaches and performance staff), common daily
241	                      tasks and responsibilities, media engagements, study and work commitments, repetitive
242	                      tasks, over-analysis, thinking about the sport in question, and environmental instability can
243	                      serve as potential causes of mental fatigue-related issues, with experience and personality
244	                      as factors of individual susceptibility [50]. Russell and colleagues [50] reported that such
245	                      issues may lead to more severe consequences, such as disengagement, decreased motivation
246	                      and enthusiasm, increased displays of emotion and withdrawal, changes in concentration,
247	                      decreased discipline and attention to detail, as previously described in reports from the elite
248	                      sporting environment, which can have a negative impact on the team staff performance if
249	                      left untreated or underappreciated.
250	                            In addition, this is an assumption as a lot of team staff members are ex-athletes and
251	                      remain quite physically active. Additionally, the stress that competition can cause to
252	                      coaching and performance personnel should be another fundamental factor to consider
253	                      elevated levels of subjective stress, alpha-amylase activity, and unpleasant emotions suggest
254	                      that educational programs may be useful for some coaches to manage psychological states
255	                      during competition [51]. A situation of combined stress for an important championship was
256	                      found to decrease the level of secretory IgA-mediated immune protection at the mucosal
257	                      surface, with greater changes observed in the athletes [52]. As such, strategies to minimize
258	                      the physiological impact are warranted.
259	
260	                      4. Recovery Considerations for Team Staff Members
261	                            The job description of the team staff members can be extensive and demanding [53].
262	                      To better cope with the challenges of daily work and with various fatigue sources, support
263	                      team staff members need to maintain a high level of health, fitness, and mental wellbeing.
264	                      Fitness, in addition to health protection, plays an important role in mental wellbeing and
265	                      adaptation to demanding cognitive and social situations [54]. Like athletes, if team staff
266	                      members possess high levels of health, fitness, and mental wellbeing, they may tolerate
267	                      fatigue better—that is to say, when in fatigued situations (physical and/or psychological),
268	                      their capacity to maintain performance will be less affected. Hence, and given the key
269	                      role of team staff members’ work outputs, and potential impact on the team’s overall
270	                      performance [44], to that extent, the importance of recovery, especially related to cognitive
271	                      and psychological fatigue, can contribute to optimizing performance outcomes.
272	                            The development of educational recovery resources for team staff members may
273	                      also help address the identified barriers and improve knowledge [3,55,56]. For example,
274	                      while team staff members have adequate overall sleep hygiene knowledge [57], some
275	                      specific areas (e.g., sleep-wake cycle behaviors) warrant further education. Sleep hygiene
276	                      education is reported to result in positive changes in sleep behavior [34,35]. However,
277	                      changes in sleep from education in an acute setting may not be sustained following the
278	                      initial intervention. The progress of instructive sleep resources for team staff members
279	                      to implement with athletes may help address the identified barriers and improve sleep
280	                      knowledge. This may be linked to the negative influence of travel, and possible time zone
281	                      changes [30,32] is another area where education would be beneficial. Empirical findings and
282	                      practical recommendations are highlighted on sleep, nutrition, recovery, and scheduling
283	                      strategies to alleviate the negative effects of air travel on health and performance [30,31,58].
284	                      Additionally, it would be helpful to have access to a sport psychologist role to address
285	                      the psychological needs of team staff members to better prepare them for the heavy and
286	                      indisputable fatigue accumulation during the season [59].
287	                            It has been previously demonstrated in athletes that planned disruptions, such as
288	                      location, competition simulation, punishments and rewards, physical strain, stronger com-
289	                      petition, distractions, unfairness or restrictions, can be used to familiarize athletes with
290	                      pressure, create awareness, develop personal resources, and promote team processes [60].
291	                      This is based on the ‘Challenge model of resilience’ presented by Fergus and Zimmer-
292	                      man [61], which suggests that exposure to some adversity can strengthen resistance against
293	                      future adversity. Consequently, this may also be a consideration to prepare support staff
